title: Counting and Causing
paragraphs: Epidemiology is often described as the science of counting, but its harder task is deciding what the counts mean. A correlation between an exposure and a disease is cheap; an argument that the exposure produces the disease is expensive, and the price is paid in alternatives ruled out rather than in data collected. The discipline's history is largely a history of learning which alternatives matter.

The episode most often cited is John Snow's investigation of the cholera outbreak around Broad Street in London in eighteen fifty four. Snow mapped deaths, noticed that they clustered near one public water pump, and persuaded local officials to remove its handle. The story is usually told as a triumph of observation over the prevailing belief that cholera spread through bad air. It was such a triumph, but a qualified one: Snow himself acknowledged that the outbreak was already declining when the handle came off, so the removal could not by itself prove his case.

What actually carried the argument was a comparison. Snow also examined households supplied by two water companies, one of which drew from a stretch of the Thames contaminated by sewage, and found far higher cholera mortality among its customers. Because the pipes of both companies ran along the same streets, the households differed in water but resembled each other in most other respects. The design did quietly what later methods would do formally: it made rival explanations implausible rather than merely unexamined.

Roughly a century later, Austin Bradford Hill proposed a set of considerations for moving from association to causation, including the strength of an association, its consistency across studies, and whether the exposure preceded the disease. They are frequently taught as a checklist. Hill, however, insisted that none of them was indispensable and that none could settle the question alone, which makes the checklist reading a curious inversion of his intent: what he offered as aids to judgment is routinely used as a substitute for it.

None of this licenses the opposite error of treating every observed link as hopelessly confounded. The lesson is narrower and more demanding: causal claims in epidemiology are earned by the patient elimination of competitors, and a count is only as informative as the alternatives it was designed to exclude.

sources.claim: John Snow 1854'te Londra'da Broad Street çevresindeki kolera salgınını inceledi, ölümlerin bir kamu su pompası yakınında kümelendiğini gösterdi ve yerel yetkilileri pompanın kolunu söktürmeye ikna etti; kolera o dönemde yaygın olarak kötü havaya (miasma) bağlanıyordu.

Snow iki su şirketinin (biri Thames'in kanalizasyonla kirlenmiş kesiminden su çeken) müşterilerini karşılaştırdı; boruları aynı sokaklarda iç içeydi ve kirli suyu alan hanelerde ölüm çok daha yüksekti; Snow salgının kol sökülmeden önce zaten azaldığını kendisi kabul etti.
